questions.prompt: Let V be two-dimensional over R with basis {v₁,v₂} and symmetric bilinear form f. Put r=f(v₁,v₁),s=f(v₁,v₂),t=f(v₂,v₂). Which statements are necessarily true?

options.B: If r=s=t, then either f(v,v)≥0 for every v or f(v,v)≤0 for every v.
options.C: If f is positive definite, then r≠s,s≠t and r≠t.
options.D: If f is positive definite, then f(v₁,v₂)=0.

hints: Write f(av₁+bv₂,av₁+bv₂)=ra²+2sab+tb².
Positive definiteness requires r>0 and rt−s²>0, not entrywise inequality or an orthogonal chosen basis.
questions.solution: Symmetry gives f(v₂,v₁)=s, so A is not necessary, e.g. s=1. If r=s=t=c, then f(av₁+bv₂,av₁+bv₂)=c(a+b)², nonnegative for c≥0 and nonpositive for c≤0; B holds. C fails for the positive-definite identity matrix, which has r=t=1,s=0. It also fails even for r≠s as an alleged requirement: [[1,1],[1,2]] is positive definite with r=s. D fails for this same matrix because f(v₁,v₂)=1. Thus only B is necessarily true.
questions.theory: A symmetric bilinear form in a chosen basis is represented by a real symmetric matrix [[r,s],[s,t]], and its associated quadratic form is ra²+2sab+tb². Positive definiteness requires a strictly positive value for every nonzero vector. In dimension two, Sylvester’s criterion is r>0 and rt−s²>0; equality of some matrix entries is entirely compatible with it. A basis for a positive-definite form need not be orthogonal, though Gram–Schmidt can produce an orthogonal basis. If all three entries equal c, the matrix has rank at most one and the quadratic form is c(a+b)², making it semidefinite with sign determined by c. Symmetric and skew-symmetric bilinear forms have different transpose identities; confusing them changes the sign of the off-diagonal entry.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the symmetric matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] positive definite?
similar_questions.solution: Its leading principal minors are 2 and 4−1=3, both positive. Equivalently its eigenvalues are 3 and 1. Thus it is positive definite despite nonzero off-diagonal entries and equal diagonal entries.

similar_questions.prompt: Classify the form with r=s=t=−2.
similar_questions.solution: The quadratic form is −2(a+b)²≤0, so it is negative semidefinite. It vanishes on the nonzero line a+b=0 and hence is not negative definite.

questions.prompt: Let f:C\{0}→C be a non-zero holomorphic function satisfying $|f(z)|\le|z|^{5/2}+|z|^{-1/2}$ for z≠0. Which statements are true?

options.A: f has a pole at z=0.
options.B: There is an entire function g equal to f on C\{0}.
options.C: f is a polynomial of degree at most 2.
options.D: f has an essential singularity at z=0.

hints: Multiply f by z to test removability at the puncture.
After extending, apply Cauchy coefficient estimates on large circles.
questions.solution: Let h(z)=zf(z). Near zero, |h(z)|≤|z|^{7/2}+|z|^{1/2}→0, so h extends holomorphically with h(0)=0 by the removable singularity theorem. Its Taylor series has a factor z, so f=h/z also extends holomorphically at zero. Thus B holds and A,D fail. For the entire extension g, Cauchy estimates on |z|=R give $|g^{(k)}(0)|/k!\le(R^{5/2}+R^{-1/2})/R^k$. For each k≥3 this tends to zero as R→∞, forcing all Taylor coefficients of degree at least three to vanish. Hence g, and therefore f on its original domain, is a polynomial of degree at most two, proving C.
questions.theory: An isolated singularity is removable when the function is bounded near it; a useful variant is to multiply by a power of z and inspect the limit. If zf extends with value zero, division of the holomorphic extension by z is still holomorphic because its Taylor series has no constant term. This excludes poles even though the original bound itself grows like |z|^(−1/2). Holomorphic pole orders are integers, so a sublinear negative-power growth cannot accommodate a genuine pole. Entire functions with polynomial growth are polynomials: Cauchy estimates send sufficiently high Taylor coefficients to zero as the radius grows. A noninteger growth exponent 5/2 allows integer degrees at most two. The near-zero and far-field parts of the bound address different conclusions and should be analyzed separately.

similar_questions.prompt: If f is holomorphic on C\{0} and |f(z)|≤|z|^{3/2}+|z|^{−1/3}, what can be concluded?
similar_questions.solution: zf(z)→0 at zero, so f extends entirely. Cauchy estimates for every k≥2 yield zero coefficients as R→∞. Thus the extension is a polynomial of degree at most one.

similar_questions.prompt: If an entire g satisfies |g(z)|≤10(1+|z|³), prove degree at most three.
similar_questions.solution: On |z|=R, Cauchy estimates give |a_k|≤10(R^{−k}+R^{3−k}). For k≥4 the right side tends to zero as R→∞, so a_k=0. The Taylor series terminates at degree three.

questions.prompt: Let D={z∈C:|z|<1} and let f:D→D be a non-constant holomorphic function with f(0)=0. For n≥1 define fₙ(z)=f(zⁿ). Which statements are true?

options.A: Σₙ≥₁ fₙ converges only at z=0.
options.B: Σₙ≥₁ fₙ converges pointwise only on a countable E⊆D and not on D\E.
options.C: Σₙ≥₁ fₙ converges pointwise everywhere in D but fails uniform convergence on some compact subsets of D.
options.D: Σₙ≥₁ fₙ converges uniformly on every compact subset of D to a holomorphic function on D.

hints: Use Schwarz’s lemma to bound |f(w)| by |w|.
Every compact subset of the disk lies in |z|≤r for some r<1; compare with a geometric series.
questions.solution: Schwarz’s lemma gives |f(w)|≤|w| for w∈D, so |fₙ(z)|≤|z|ⁿ. For a compact K⊆D choose r=max_{z∈K}|z|<1. Then sup_K|fₙ|≤rⁿ and Σrⁿ converges. The Weierstrass M-test proves absolute uniform convergence on K. In particular the series converges at every point of D, refuting A,B. Each fₙ is holomorphic, and locally uniform convergence of their partial sums makes the sum holomorphic. Thus D holds and C fails.
questions.theory: Schwarz’s lemma applies to a holomorphic self-map of the unit disk fixing zero and gives the pointwise estimate |f(z)|≤|z|. Substituting z^n turns this into a geometric bound. Compact subsets of an open disk have a strict radial bound r<1, because the continuous modulus attains a maximum there and no point reaches the boundary. The Weierstrass M-test then gives uniform absolute convergence on each compact set. Such locally uniform convergence of holomorphic functions preserves holomorphy; it also permits termwise differentiation on smaller compact neighborhoods, though a separate derivative bound is needed for direct uniform derivative convergence. Uniform convergence on all of D is a stronger property and is not claimed: for f(z)=z the resulting geometric series behaves poorly as z approaches 1.

similar_questions.prompt: For f(z)=z, sum Σₙ≥₁f(zⁿ) on |z|<1 and discuss convergence.
similar_questions.solution: The series is Σzⁿ=z/(1−z). It converges uniformly on every |z|≤r<1 by the geometric bound, and the sum is holomorphic in the disk.

similar_questions.prompt: For f(z)=z², sum Σₙ≥₁f(zⁿ) and give a tail bound on |z|≤r<1.
similar_questions.solution: The series is Σz^{2n}=z²/(1−z²). After N terms the tail has magnitude at most Σₙ>N r^{2n}=r^{2N+2}/(1−r²), tending uniformly to zero.
